newsitem.title: USA: Official defends not charging Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Official defends not charging Merrill.

text.p: Assistant U.S. Attorney Brien O'Connor on Friday defended his office's decision not to seek criminal charges against Merrill Lynch & Co Inc at the same time it filed such charges against former municipal banker Mark Ferber.

U.S. Judge William Young in December sentenced Ferber to 33 months in prison and a $1 million fine after a jury convicted him in August on fraud and corruption charges. The court found Ferber failed to disclose to financial advisory clients a secret kickback contract between Merrill and his employer, Lazard Freres & Co.
Merrill and Lazard settled with the U.S. Attorney's office in late 1995 on the matter, paying a total of $24 million in civil fines.
Neither firm admitted or denied guilt in the case.
Judge Young blasted Merrill Lynch at Ferber's sentencing hearing on Dec 19. "Merrill Lynch paid the money. Merrill Lynch bought its way out for $12 million," Young said angrily.

Young said the deal between Merrill and Lazard was a "kickback scheme...and kickbacks don't fall out of the sky....He (Ferber) leaned on them (Merrill). He was at the gate -- and they played him for a sucker."

But speaking at a conference of the American Bar Association's Litigation Section here, O'Connor said Merrill Lynch, unlike Ferber, did not have a "fiduciary" duty to the municipalities involved and, therefore, "by law did not have the same obligation that Ferber had."
O'Connor added, "From a strategic, gut, factual standpoint, it was Ferber who initiated all of the corrupt, wrongful conduct in the case."
He said, "Ferber was saying (to Merrill) I want you to do this for me or things will not go well for you. Merrill was one of the parties on the receiving end of that conduct by Ferber."
O'Connor added that "it was just a very small part of Merrill Lynch's business that was involved in the conduct."
Under federal law, if a securities firm is indicted on criminal charges and found guilty, the entire firm can lose its license to do securities business.

"Were we to indict Merrill as an institution, (its) counsel could make a good argument that it could even lead to an unraveling of the whole company," O'Connor said, adding that happened with Drexel Burnham Lambert Inc and E.F. Hutton & Co.

O'Connor said, "Merrill Lynch agreed to pay at least as much as what it would have had to pay in criminal fines if it had been indicted and convicted. We also got Merrill to agree voluntarily to change certain practices."
He added, "We did not think it would be fair, in the final analysis, to charge the company and perhaps lose all of the good services that Merrill Lynch provides around this country and the world."
